title: Coronavirus (COVID-19) roundup, 27 April to 1 May 2020
meta_description: Data and analysis related to the coronavirus (COVID-19) pandemic and its impact on our economy and society.
lede: Data and analysis related to the coronavirus (COVID-19) pandemic and its impact on our economy and society.

body.text: This page contains data and analysis published by the Office for National Statistics (ONS) from 27 April to 1 May 2020. Go to our [live page](https://www.ons.gov.uk/peoplepopulationandcommunity/healthandsocialcare/conditionsanddiseases/articles/coronaviruscovid19roundup/2020-03-26) for the most up-to-date insights on COVID-19.

body.h2: Deaths involving COVID-19 by local area
body.text: Deaths involving COVID-19 by local area

body.h2: Deaths involving COVID-19 by local area
body.text: We have analysed all deaths involving the coronavirus (COVID-19) that occurred in England and Wales between 1 March and 17 April 2020 (registered up to 18 April 2020), [focusing on differences between local areas](http://www.ons.gov.uk/peoplepopulationandcommunity/birthsdeathsandmarriages/deaths/bulletins/deathsinvolvingcovid19bylocalareasanddeprivation/deathsoccurringbetween1marchand17april).

body.h2: Deaths involving COVID-19 by local area
body.text: The local authorities with the highest age-standardised mortality rates for deaths involving COVID-19 were all London boroughs, led by Newham (144.3 deaths per 100,000 population), Brent (141.5) and Hackney (127.4).

body.h2: Deaths involving COVID-19 by local area
body.text: Overall, London had 85.7 COVID-19 deaths per 100,000 population, almost double the rate of the next worst-affected region (West Midlands at 43.2). The South West had the lowest age-standardised mortality rate, at 16.4 deaths per 100,000 people.

body.text: If we categorise areas by levels of deprivation, we find that deaths involving COVID-19 had occurred at more than twice the rate in the most deprived neighbourhoods in England (55.1 deaths per 100,000 people) compared with the least deprived (25.3).

body.h2: Technology and homeworking
body.text: Technology and homeworking

body.h2: Technology and homeworking
body.text: Technology is helping to enable large numbers of people to work from home during the coronavirus (COVID-19) lockdown – but the ability to do so varies a lot between industries.

body.h2: Technology and homeworking
body.text: In 2019, only 10% of employees in the accommodation and food services industry had ever worked from home, compared with 53% in the information and communication industry.

body.h2: Technology and homeworking
body.text: Some jobs require face-to-face contact, or access to tools and machinery, and it may never be possible to work from home. But having access to the right equipment can make a difference. Our E-Commerce Survey shows that in 2018, outside the information and communication industry, less than half of employees were provided with a portable device (like a phone, tablet or laptop).

body.h2: Technology and homeworking
body.text: Our article, [technology intensity and homeworking in the UK](http://www.ons.gov.uk/employmentandlabourmarket/peopleinwork/employmentandemployeetypes/articles/technologyintensityandhomeworkingintheuk/2020-05-01), looks at how technology can allow some people to work remotely.
